doc.title: Frank Alkyer interviewed by Monk Rowe, New Orleans, Louisiana, January 10, 2020

title: DownBeat's 1934 founding, Benny Goodman and the early newsy years
summary: Alkyer says DownBeat began as a newsletter by a life-insurance salesman, then focused on Benny Goodman's rise. Its early coverage was freewheeling and included union boss Petrillo.

story.theme_name: Working for Benny Goodman: the leader and his bands
story.community_name: Working for Benny Goodman: the perfectionist bandleader

blocks.x: 1934. Do you think you have a similar mission statement now?
I didn’t know I made a joke.

Well in 1934 there was no mission statement believe you me. You know the first issue I think was eight pages long and it was basically a listing of all the bands and where they were playing and who was in the bands, because the guy who started the magazine sold life insurance policies to the — he was also a saxophone player on the side — but he sold life insurance. And he wanted to keep track of his clients. So DownBeat started as a little newsletter for this guy who sold life insurance. So there was not much of a mission statement other than hey, how do I keep track of my clients in 1934. That changed pretty quickly in 1935 when this guy named Benny Goodman, this kid became an overnight sensation across the country. And Benny Goodman is from Chicago, DownBeat was a hometown magazine, we had the inside story, all boats were rising with Benny Goodman. And that became DownBeat’s reason to be, covering Benny Goodman, covering everything he’s doing in those early days. Really, really, really. It was like Rolling Stone covering the Beatles in the 1960s. It was that kind of an element that thrust it forward. So the mission statement became pretty clear pretty quickly. But you know they were not

journalists, they were musicians mostly. They were cantankerous, they were, you know it was, there was some funny stuff that would go on. And I wish that we could do some of that. And sometimes we try to get an element of it, but we just can’t be quite that freewheeling when you’re 85 years old and you’ve been around for all this time. We have a little bit more weight and gravitas that we need to present in the magazine, so —

Plus those big bands provided such drama. I have some from the mid-40s and first of all the look of them is just so wonderful. But these titles, like: “Dorsey Hires New Canary.” And the language. And the orks, they called them orks for orchestra.
And some guy left some band for some other band it was like —

Yeah. It was a [gestures] connect the dots, connect the dots. Yeah. It was a much different thing. It was really, well you’ve got to think, they, it was very newsy. And James C. Petrillo, you know, the union boss in Chicago, we were covering how Petrillo was trying to make musicians do things they shouldn’t be doing, and James C. Petrillo was a man who had a huge ego. The C stood for Caesar. His middle name was Caesar. And he acted like a “Caesar” in those days. So yeah, you had all these like stories. It was really — they were trying to figure out what they were. It probably wasn’t until the later 1940s and into the 1950s that DownBeat became kind of like, that its mission started to become present. And they said okay, now we’ve been around for a while, here are the things we should do, and thoughtful journalism and really, really good writers and that kind of thing. In those early days it was pretty freewheeling.
